Question 1
?

Let c=⟨−2,0,0⟩ and d=⟨4,−1,0⟩. Find the scalar projection of c onto d.

a
17
b
−4
c
0
d
−817
e
−2
Submit

decision.explanation: The scalar projection is (c·d)/||d||. Here c·d = (-2)(4) = -8 and ||d|| = √(4²+(-1)²) = √17, so the scalar projection is -8/√17.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Let $c=⟨-2,0,0⟩$ and $d=⟨4,-1,0⟩.$ Find the scalar projection of $c$ onto $d.$
after.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}+{d}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-2\cdot 4+0\cdot (-1)+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
content.problem: Let $a=⟨3,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨3,4,1⟩.$ Find the scalar projection of $a$ onto $b.$
content.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 3+2\cdot 4+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{18}{\sqrt{26}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The scalar projection is (p·q)/||q||. Since q is nonzero, a zero projection requires p·q = -4 + x + 2 = x - 2 = 0. Thus x = 2.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Let $p=⟨-1,1,2⟩$ and $q=⟨4,x,1⟩.$ Given that the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q$ is zero, find the value of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 4+1\cdot x+2\cdot 1 \\  & =x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Since p is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector q equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular.

So, we must have

p⊥q⟹p⋅q=0.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Let $p=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $q=[\begin{aligned}x \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ Given that the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q$ is $0,$ find the value of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =6\cdot x+1\cdot 4+4\cdot (-4) \\  & =6x-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ 6x-12 & =0 \\ 6x & =12 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}

Since p is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector q equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular.

So, we must have

p⊥q⟹p⋅q=0.

content.knowledge_point: Projecting a Vector Onto a Perpendicular Vector
content.problem: Let $p=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $q=[\begin{aligned}x \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ Given that the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q$ is $0,$ find the value of $x.$
content.worked_solution:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =6\cdot x+1\cdot 4+4\cdot (-4) \\  & =6x-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ 6x-12 & =0 \\ 6x & =12 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
